slides.title: Exceptions

blocks.text: Exceptions are runtime errors. The JVM detects an operation that is impossible to carry out.
Exception handling enables a program to handle runtime errors and continue its normal execution.
For example, if you divide an integer by 0, you will get an
ArithmeticException.
If you enter a double value when your program expects an integer, you will get an InputMismatchException.
If you access an array using an index that is out of bounds, you
will get an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

slides.title: Catching the Exception

blocks.text: If number2 is 0, the quotient method throws an exception:
throw new ArithmeticException("Divisor cannot be zero");
The exception is an object created from an exception class. In this case:
java.lang.ArithmeticException.
The constructor ArithmeticException(str) is invoked to construct an exception object, where str is a string that describes the exception.
When an exception is thrown, execution flow is interrupted.
The try block contains the code that is executed in normal circumstances, when there is no exception.
The exception is caught by the catch block. The code in the catch block is executed to handle the exception.

slides.title: Exception Advantages

blocks.text: Exception handling enables a method to throw an exception to its caller, enabling the caller to handle the exception.
Often the called method does not know what to do in case of an exception.
This is the case for the library methods. The library method can detect the error, but only the caller knows what needs to be done when an exception occurs.
The key benefit is separating the detection of an exception
(done in a called method) from the handling of an exception (done in the calling method).

slides.title: Exception Types

blocks.text: Exceptions are classes in the Java API. The root class for exceptions is java.lang.Throwable.
Exceptions thrown are instances of the exception classes.
Exception is caused by your program and external circumstances. These can be caught and handled by your program.
Error is an internal system error thrown by the JVM. Rarely occurs but terminates program execution.
RuntimeException is caused
by programming errors, such as numeric errors and bad indexing.

slides.title: Exception Types

blocks.text: Throwable is the root class of all exception classes. All Java exception classes inherit directly or indirectly from Throwable.
The Error class describes internal system errors that are thrown by the JVM,
such as LinkageError and VirtualMachineError.
The ClassNotFoundException occurs if you run a nonexistent class.
The IOException is related to input/output operations, such as invalid input, reading past the end of a file, and opening a nonexistent file.
ArithmeticException occurs if you divide an integer by zero.
NullPointerException if you access an object through a null reference.
IndexOutOfBoundsException occurs if you index an array out of range.
IllegalArgumentException if you pass an illegal argument to a method.

slides.title: Unchecked versus Checked Exceptions

blocks.text: RuntimeException, Error, and their subclasses are known as unchecked exceptions.
In most cases, unchecked exceptions reflect programming logic errors that should be corrected by the programmer.
Unchecked exceptions can occur anywhere in the program.
To avoid cumbersome overuse of try-catch blocks, Java does not force you to write code to catch unchecked exceptions.
All other exceptions are known as checked exceptions, meaning that the compiler forces the programmer to check and deal with the exceptions.

slides.title: Unchecked Exceptions

blocks.text: In most cases, unchecked exceptions reflect programming logic errors that should be corrected in the program.
For example, a NullPointerException is thrown if you access an object through a null reference variable before an object is assigned to it.
An IndexOutOfBoundsException is thrown if you access an array element outside the bounds of the array.
Unchecked exceptions can occur anywhere in the program.
To avoid overuse of the try-catch blocks, Java does not mandate you to write code to catch unchecked exceptions.

slides.title: When to Use Exceptions

blocks.text: A method should throw an exception if the error needs to be handled by the caller.
Exception handling separates error-handling from normal code, making programs easier to read and modify.
If you can handle the exception in the method where it occurs, there is no need to throw or use exceptions.
Use the try-catch block to deal with unexpected error conditions. Do not use it to deal with simple errors.
Simple errors are best handled without throwing exceptions.

slides.title: Defining a Custom Exception Class

blocks.text: Use the Java exception classes whenever possible.
Define your own custom exception class if the predefined exception classes in the Java language are not sufficient.
Define an exception class by extending the Java Exception class or one of its subclasses, such as IOException.
For example, the setRadius method throws the
IllegalArgumentException if radius is negative.
Suppose you want to pass the radius to the handler. Then, you can define a custom InvalidRadiusException.
